So I was watching Boogie's thoughts on that Tracer Butt issue and his mellow, well reasoned tone got me thinking about this.

Way in the past, games, even with big hype machines behind them, had previews in magazines and such. We had to be content with a few choice screenshots printed on paper. If the release was really far away, a lot of time we only got one, maybe two screenshots each the size of two postage stamps or so. Sometimes they'd get a few pages with an in-depth preview but, for the most part, it was a few words and pictures on a one-way communication medium.

A decade ago there were torrents and mountains of preview videos, rumors, screenshots (and bullshots) of the highest resolutions and qualities. These days it's one better with anyone with time and luck can get access to large public betas, both closed and open. Some companies put their unfinished games out and call it early access and let people buy into it so they can be among the first and being able to brag later about being the first when it was still unknown. And there's social media and forums to make things a two-way dialog.

Now, Blizzard claims they were always intending to modify Tracer's pose and I found that a very suspicious thing to be said and done after a complaint on Battle.net. I'm not saying they're lying but I have to wonder if everyone, including the original complainer, is being honest about who they are.

Thing is, in the past, art assets would absolutely go through iterations just like code does, but no one really got to see those iterations. Sites like The Cutting Room Floor seem to thrive on wringing every drop of blood from the stone they possibly can to find peeks into the development and iterative process. With very very few exceptions, the game that was available for purchase on release day is absolutely 100% the result of the company saying "that's good enough" and pushing it out the door, and without the ability to patch, what they made couldn't later be sanitized.

They say you shouldn't see sausage being made, so I've got to think that this new era of exposed development has opened a lot of opportunity for busybodies to coerce, manipulate, and encourage development teams to compromise their artistic vision for the sake of avoiding backlash and criticism (simply perceived or otherwise legitimate). Patch-it-later development and required updates leads to games like Skullgirls changing art and pulling essentially a bait and switch.

tl;dr Has a more transparent development cycle encouraged hyper-criticism and excessive sensitivity and muddies the waters when companies claim "artistic vision" when self-censoring content?
Do early-access games and beta tests open the doors for self-censorship in a way that previous game generations did not?
